2027-05-30.title: The Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ (Corpus Christi)
readings: See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you
I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord (or: Alleluia)
How much more will the blood of Christ … purify our conscience from dead works to worship the living God!
Praise, O Zion, praise your Saviour (shorter form from Ecce panis angelorum, Behold the bread of angels)
This is my body. This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many
2027-05-30.alt: Solemnity. Year B. In India the Latin Church keeps Corpus Christi on this Sunday, and so the Ninth Sunday in Ordinary Time is not celebrated; where the solemnity is kept on Thursday (as at the Vatican and in many countries), it was celebrated on 27 May. Gloria and Creed. The Sequence Lauda Sion may be sung before the Gospel Acclamation, in full or in the shorter form. Where possible, a procession with the Blessed Sacrament follows the Mass, ending with Benediction. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-05-30.verse: While they were eating, he took a loaf of bread, and after blessing it he broke it, gave it to them, and said, “Take; this is my body.” Then he took a cup, and after giving thanks he gave it to them, and all of them drank from it.
theo: On this Sunday the Church kneels before the gift that Jesus left on the night before he died: his own Body and Blood. In Holy Week we remembered the Last Supper in the shadow of the Passion. Today, in the light of Easter and Pentecost, we celebrate the same gift with open joy, carry it through our streets and adore it. The readings of Year B have one thread running through all of them: blood and covenant. The first reading takes us to the foot of Mount Sinai. Moses has come down and “told the people all the words of the LORD and all the ordinances; and all the people answered with one voice, and said, ‘All the words that the LORD has spoken we will do.’” Then he builds an altar with twelve pillars, one for each tribe. Young men offer sacrifices, and Moses does something that seems strange to us: he takes half of the blood and dashes it against the altar, which stands for God, and after reading the book of the covenant aloud and hearing the people promise again, he dashes the other half on the people, saying: “See the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.” For the people of the Bible, blood is life. The same life now touches both the altar and the people: God and Israel are bound together like blood relatives, one family. That is what a covenant means. The Psalm is the song of one who has been rescued and asks how to give thanks: “What shall I return to the LORD for all his bounty to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD.” Christians have always heard in it the voice of the Church at every Mass.

The Letter to the Hebrews explains what Moses' ceremony was pointing to. The high priest of the old covenant entered the Holy of Holies once a year with the blood of animals. “But when Christ came as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation), he entered once for all into the Holy Place, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, thus obtaining eternal redemption.” The author reasons from the lesser to the greater: if the blood of animals could make people outwardly clean for worship, “how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to worship the living God!” Notice that the whole Trinity is at work: Christ offers himself, through the eternal Spirit, to God the Father. And the result is a new covenant: “For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance.” Moses sprinkled blood on the outside of the people. Christ's blood reaches the conscience, the inner heart, and makes us able to worship the living God.

The Gospel brings us into the upper room. Jesus sends two disciples into the city: “a man carrying a jar of water will meet you; follow him,” and he will show them “a large room upstairs, furnished and ready.” The Lord himself prepares the place of the meal. That evening, while they are eating the Passover, “he took a loaf of bread, and after blessing it he broke it, gave it to them, and said, ‘Take; this is my body.’ Then he took a cup, and after giving thanks he gave it to them, and all of them drank from it. He said to them, ‘This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.’” The disciples, good Jews who knew Exodus 24, could not miss the echo: the blood of the covenant. What Moses sprinkled from a basin, Jesus gives to drink, and it is his own blood. He does not say: this is a sign of my body; he says: this is my body. The Church has always taken him at his word. By the power of the Holy Spirit and the words of Christ spoken by the priest, the whole substance of the bread becomes the Body of Christ and the whole substance of the wine becomes his Blood, while the appearances of bread and wine remain; the Church calls this change transubstantiation (Council of Trent; Catechism 1376). Christ is present in the Eucharist truly, really and substantially, Body and Blood, soul and divinity. And because the Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of the cross, the Mass is not only a meal but the sacrifice of the new covenant. The Gospel ends simply: “When they had sung the hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.” The hymn was probably the Hallel psalms, which include today's Psalm 116. From the table Jesus goes out to give his body and pour out his blood. Today we too go out from the altar in procession, carrying him through our towns and villages, so that the whole world may see the One who gave his life for many.
conn: The phrase in Exodus 24:8 is repeated by Jesus in Mark 14:24 and recalled at every Mass. In the Bible a covenant is not a contract but a family bond; blood shared by the altar and the people makes them kin. Jesus seals the new covenant with his own blood.
Moses sets up twelve pillars for the twelve tribes (Exodus 24:4). At the Last Supper Jesus sits with the Twelve, the foundation of the renewed Israel, the Church.
“A man carrying a jar of water.”
Carrying water was usually women's work, so a man with a jar would be easy to recognise. The Lord himself prepares everything for the meal, as he still prepares the altar for us.

The Last Supper took place in the setting of the Passover, the memorial of Israel's liberation from Egypt, when the blood of the lamb saved the firstborn (Exodus 12). Jesus is the true Paschal Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Jesus does not say “this represents” but “this is.” The Church teaches that the whole substance of bread and wine is changed into the substance of the Body and Blood of Christ (transubstantiation), while the appearances remain (Catechism 1376).

An echo of the Servant in Isaiah 53:12, who “poured out himself to death” and “bore the sin of many.” In Hebrew idiom “many” means the great multitude, without limit; Christ died for all (Catechism 605).
Hebrews compares the earthly tabernacle, where the high priest entered once a year, with heaven itself, where Christ has entered once for all with his own blood (Hebrews 9:24).
At the end of the Passover meal Jews sang the second part of the Hallel, Psalms 115–118; Psalm 116, today's Psalm, belongs to it. Jesus sang the Psalms on his way to the Passion.

The feast arose in the thirteenth century in Liège, through the visions of St Juliana of Cornillon, and was extended to the whole Church by Pope Urban IV in 1264. St Thomas Aquinas composed its Office and the Sequence Lauda Sion.
altar: What Moses dashed from a basin and Jesus gave in the upper room is given to us today at this altar. The bread and wine we bring become, by the power of the Holy Spirit and the words of Christ, his true Body and Blood. We do not receive a symbol but the living Lord, Body and Blood, soul and divinity.

The Mass is the sacrifice of the new covenant: the one offering of Christ on the cross made present, not repeated. That is why we adore the Blessed Sacrament after Mass, in the tabernacle and in the monstrance, and carry him in procession: the same Lord who was offered for us remains with us.
outline: Ask: if you saw Jesus carried through your street today, what would you do? Kneel, look away, or follow?
Point 1 · The blood of the covenant
At Sinai blood touches altar and people: God makes Israel his family.
Point 2 · How much more the blood of Christ
Christ enters heaven with his own blood and purifies our conscience.
In the upper room Jesus gives himself, truly present, the sacrifice of the new covenant.
From the altar to the street: adoration, procession, mission.
A small white Host in a golden monstrance, carried slowly down a village road, and people kneeling on both sides.
live: This week, spend ten minutes before the Blessed Sacrament in your parish church, or in an adoration chapel, simply looking at him and letting him look at you.
Before Mass next Sunday, prepare with a short examination of conscience, keep the Eucharistic fast, and go to confession if you are in serious sin.
If your parish holds a Eucharistic procession, walk in it with your family; if not, kneel in silence at the moment of Benediction.
Do not rush out after Mass. Stay two minutes after receiving Holy Communion to thank him, using the words of the Psalm: What shall I return to the Lord?
fathers: Do not regard the bread and wine as bare elements, for they are the Body and Blood of Christ according to the Lord's own declaration. Even if the senses suggest otherwise, let faith make you sure. Judge not by taste but by faith.

The word of Christ, which could make out of nothing what did not exist, can it not change things that exist into what they were not? It is no less to give new natures to things than to change their natures.

In the hymn Adoro te devote he prays: sight, touch and taste are deceived in you, but hearing alone is trusted; I believe whatever the Son of God has said, for nothing is truer than this word of Truth.
magis: Christ is present in the Eucharist truly, really and substantially, Body and Blood, soul and divinity.
The Council of Trent: by consecration the whole substance of bread and wine is changed into the Body and Blood of Christ; this change is called transubstantiation.
The Eucharist is the memorial of Christ's Passover and a true sacrifice: the one sacrifice of the cross made present.
Worship of the Eucharist: adoration of the Blessed Sacrament inside and outside Mass, and processions.
Lumen Gentium 11; St John Paul II, Ecclesia de Eucharistia 1
The Eucharist is the source and summit of the whole Christian life; the Church draws her life from the Eucharist.
saints: St Juliana of Cornillon (d. 1258), a nun near Liège, longed for a feast of the Blessed Sacrament; the bishop of Liège first kept it in 1246. Pope Urban IV extended it to the whole Church in 1264 (bull Transiturus), and St Thomas Aquinas wrote its Office. In India the solemnity is kept on the Sunday after Trinity.

31 May: the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary (feast), close of the Marian month. 1 Jun: St Justin, martyr. 3 Jun: Sts Charles Lwanga and companions, martyrs. 4 Jun: the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus (solemnity). 5 Jun: the Immaculate Heart of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
2027-05-30.prayer: O God, who in this wonderful Sacrament have left us a memorial of your Passion, grant us, we pray, so to revere the sacred mysteries of your Body and Blood that we may always experience in ourselves the fruits of your redemption. Who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, true God and true man, hidden under the appearance of bread and wine, we adore you. You sealed the new covenant with your own blood; purify our conscience to worship the living God. What shall we return to you for all your goodness? We will lift up the cup of salvation and call on your name. Walk with us through our streets today, bless our homes, and make us one body in you. Amen.

quick: At Sinai Moses sealed the covenant by dashing blood on the altar and on the people: See the blood of the covenant.
Christ, our high priest, entered heaven with his own blood, and his blood purifies our conscience to worship the living God.
At the Last Supper Jesus took bread and the cup and said: This is my body; this is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many.
2027-05-30.action: Spend ten minutes this week in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament.
2027-05-30.question: Do I receive Holy Communion as if I truly believed that it is Jesus himself?
catechism: The real presence of Christ in the Eucharist.
Why do we adore the Blessed Sacrament?
kidsaint: Carlo was a boy in Italy who loved computers, video games and his dog. But most of all he loved Jesus in the Eucharist. He went to Mass every day he could, and he called the Eucharist his highway to heaven. He used his computer skills to make a website about Eucharistic miracles from all over the world, so that more people would believe that Jesus is really there. He died of leukaemia when he was only fifteen, in 2006, and Pope Leo XIV declared him a saint in 2025. Lesson: you can love Jesus in the Eucharist with all your heart, even while you are young and enjoy ordinary things.
2027-05-30.special: Solemnity of the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ (Year B), kept on this Sunday in India in place of the Ninth Sunday in Ordinary Time. Gloria and Creed. Sequence Lauda Sion (optional). Eucharistic procession and Benediction where possible.
term: The word the Church uses for the change that takes place at the consecration of the Mass: the whole substance of the bread becomes the Body of Christ and the whole substance of the wine becomes his Blood, while the appearances (colour, taste, shape) of bread and wine remain (Council of Trent; Catechism 1376). Jesus is therefore present not as a symbol but truly, really and substantially.

family.explain: At the Last Supper Jesus took bread and said: this is my body. He took the cup and said: this is my blood. Jesus gave himself to his friends, and he still gives himself to us at every Mass. The Host looks like bread, but it is really Jesus. That is why we kneel, we are quiet, and we say Amen when we receive him.
family.intention: We pray for children preparing for their First Holy Communion, and for all who cannot go to Mass because they are sick or far away.
family.ask: Ask: “How can our family show Jesus that we believe he is really present in the Holy Eucharist?” Then plan a short family visit to the Blessed Sacrament this week.

illus: In a coastal parish near Kollam the Corpus Christi procession used to pass the house of an old fisherman who had not been to church for thirty years. Every year his neighbours put out lamps and flowers; he sat on his veranda with his back turned. One year, when the monstrance stopped for Benediction right in front of his gate, his little granddaughter ran out and knelt in the road. He went out to bring her back, and found himself kneeling beside her. The next week he went to confession. He said afterwards: I had stopped going to him, so he came to me. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord Jesus, truly present in the Most Holy Sacrament, we adore you. Gather us around your table and make us one body in you. Amen.
share: See the blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:8). What does it mean to me that God has made me part of his family by the blood of Christ?
How much more will the blood of Christ purify our conscience (Hebrews 9:14). Do I bring to the Eucharist a heart that wants to be purified?
Take; this is my body (Mark 14:22). How do I prepare for Holy Communion, and how do I give thanks afterwards?
pm.resp: I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord.
interc: For the Church, that she may always draw her life from the Eucharist and adore the Lord with deep faith.
For priests, who stand at the altar in the person of Christ, that they may celebrate the holy mysteries with reverence and love.
For children preparing for First Holy Communion, and for their parents and catechists.
For the sick, the elderly and prisoners who cannot come to Mass, that they may receive the Lord through those who bring Communion.
For the hungry of our country, that those who receive the Bread of Life may share their bread.
pm.close: Father, your Son gave us his Body and Blood as the food of eternal life. May we who receive him become what we receive. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today the Church kneels in wonder before the greatest gift Jesus left us: his own Body and Blood. In many of our parishes the Blessed Sacrament will be carried through the streets this evening, with candles, flowers, songs and children in white. We do this because we believe that the small white Host is not a thing but a Person: Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

In the first reading Moses stands at the foot of Mount Sinai. The people promise: all that the Lord has spoken we will do. Moses takes the blood of the sacrifice, dashes half of it on the altar and half on the people, and says: see the blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:8). For the people of the Bible, blood is life. The same life touches God's altar and God's people. Now they are one family. That is a covenant.

But that covenant was written in the blood of animals, and the people did not keep their promise. So God made a new covenant. The Letter to the Hebrews says: Christ entered once for all into the Holy Place, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood (Hebrews 9:12). And his blood does what animal blood could never do: it purifies our conscience from dead works to worship the living God (Hebrews 9:14). It washes not our skin but our heart.

Then the Gospel. In the upper room Jesus takes bread and says: take; this is my body. He takes the cup and says: this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many (Mark 14:22, 24). The apostles remembered Moses. What Moses sprinkled, Jesus gives to drink, and it is his own blood. He did not say: this is a picture of my body. He said: this is my body. And the Church believes him. The bread becomes his Body, the wine becomes his Blood. It still looks like bread, it still tastes like wine, but it is the Lord.

If we truly believe this, it will change how we come to Mass. We will come on time. We will prepare our hearts, and go to confession when we have sinned seriously. We will receive him with reverence, and say Amen with faith. And we will not run away after Communion, but stay a few moments to thank him. As the Psalm says: what shall I return to the Lord for all his bounty to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation.

Finally the Gospel says: when they had sung the hymn, they went out (Mark 14:26). Jesus went out to give his life. Today we go out in procession, carrying him through our streets, so that our neighbours may see the One who loves them. And when we go home, we carry him too, in our hearts. Let us become what we receive: the Body of Christ, broken and shared for the world. Amen.
kids: Children, at the Last Supper Jesus took bread and said: this is my body. Then he took the cup and said: this is my blood. Jesus loves us so much that he wants to come right into our hearts! At Mass the bread and wine become Jesus himself. It still looks like bread, but it is really Jesus.

So when you see the Host lifted up at Mass, or carried in the procession today, say quietly in your heart: My Lord and my God! And if you have made your First Holy Communion, when you receive Jesus, say thank you to him with all your heart.

opts.a: A large room, furnished and ready
intro: Before the Last Supper Jesus sent two disciples to prepare a room. Today he asks us to prepare a place for him: in our churches, in our homes and in our hearts.

points.h: Where do you want us to go?
sub: Jesus has already chosen the place.
points.apply: Ask Jesus in prayer where he wants to meet you this week.

points.h: Follow the man with the jar
sub: A strange sign in the city.
points.apply: Follow one instruction of the Church you have been neglecting.
Keep the Eucharistic fast carefully and come to Mass early to prepare.

concl: The Lord who gives himself in the Eucharist asks for a prepared place.
A heart made ready receives him with faith and love.
opts.resolve: This week I will prepare for Communion with prayer, confession if needed, and the Eucharistic fast.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today's Gospel begins not with the Last Supper itself but with the preparations. On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb is sacrificed, his disciples said to him: where do you want us to go and make the preparations for you to eat the Passover? (Mark 14:12). They asked. Jesus had already chosen the place.

The Book of Proverbs pictures Wisdom building her house and setting her table, and calling: come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed (Proverbs 9:5). Jesus is the Wisdom of God. He has prepared the table long before we arrive. But he wants us to prepare too. Each Sunday the question of the disciples is ours: Lord, where do you want me to meet you?

Jesus gives a strange sign: go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you; follow him (Mark 14:13). In those days men rarely carried water jars; it was the work of women. The disciples had to obey before they understood. Isaiah had called: everyone who thirsts, come to the waters (Isaiah 55:1). Sometimes the way to the Eucharist is through simple obedience: to the Sunday obligation, to the one-hour fast, to confession when we have sinned seriously.

Then: he will show you a large room upstairs, furnished and ready. Make preparations for us there (Mark 14:15). The room was ready, but the disciples still had to prepare the meal. The psalm says: you prepare a table before me (Psalm 23:5). God prepares; we prepare. How do we prepare our hearts? With a short prayer before Mass, by arriving early, by an act of contrition, by keeping the Eucharistic fast, by a moment of silent thanks after Communion.

So the disciples set out and went to the city, and found everything as he had told them (Mark 14:16). If we prepare, we will find everything as he promised: the Lord himself, truly present, waiting for us. Let us prepare our churches beautifully, our homes for the procession, and above all our hearts for every Mass. Amen.

opts.a: From the altar to the street
intro: The Lord we receive at the altar is the same Lord we must recognise in the poor. Corpus Christi joins adoration and charity.

points.apply: Spend half an hour in adoration this week.

sub: The mediator of a new covenant.
points.apply: After Communion, ask the Lord to change one thing in your heart.

points.h: The same Lord in the poor
sub: Open your hand to the needy.
points.apply: Do one concrete act of charity this week as the fruit of your Communion.

concl: The Eucharist makes us dwell in Christ and Christ in us.
Whoever adores him at the altar must serve him in the poor.
opts.resolve: This week I will spend time in adoration and serve Christ in one poor person.
homily: Dear friends, today we carry the Blessed Sacrament through our streets. The procession is a picture of the whole Christian life: we begin at the altar and we go out to the street. Let us reflect on that journey.

It begins with communion. Jesus said: those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them (John 6:56). To abide means to stay, to make a home. Jesus does not come to us as a visitor who leaves. He wants to make his home in us. The psalm says: O taste and see that the LORD is good (Psalm 34:8). In adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, we learn to stay with him as he stays with us.

The second reading calls Christ the mediator of a new covenant (Hebrews 9:15). Jeremiah had promised: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). The old covenant was written on stone; the new covenant is written on hearts, and the Eucharist is how God writes. Each Communion, received with faith, changes us a little: we become more patient, more pure, more generous.

And that change must show in the street. St Paul warned that those who eat and drink without discerning the body bring judgment on themselves. St John Chrysostom told his people: do you want to honour the body of Christ? Do not ignore him when he is naked; do not honour him here in church with silk and then neglect him outside, where he is cold and naked. Jesus said: just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40). Moses commanded: open your hand to the poor and needy neighbor in your land (Deuteronomy 15:11).

So let us adore him at the altar and serve him in the street. Spend time in adoration this week. Ask him after Communion to write his law on your heart. And let every Mass end in one act of charity for someone in need. Then the procession will not end today; it will continue every day of our lives. Amen.

intro: The blood of the covenant at Sinai, the blood of Christ that purifies the conscience, and the gift of the upper room carried into our streets.

sub: Blood on altar and people: one family.
q: Moses took the blood and dashed it on the people, and said, “See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you in accordance with all these words.”
He said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.”
points.apply: At the consecration this week, when the chalice is raised, say inwardly: Lord, by your blood I belong to your family.

points.h: How much more the blood of Christ
sub: The high priest and the Holy of Holies.
Once for all, with his own blood.
q: For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you for making atonement for your lives on the altar;
how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to worship the living God!
points.apply: Make a good confession before you next receive Communion if you are aware of serious sin, so that the Lord may purify your conscience.

q: What shall I return to the Lord for all his bounty to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord,
The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?
points.apply: Stay at least two minutes in silent thanksgiving after every Holy Communion this month.

sub: The hymn and the Mount of Olives.
q: I will pay my vows to the Lord in the presence of all his people,
Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
points.apply: After the procession, share a meal or some food this week with a family or person in need, so that the Bread of Life becomes bread shared.

concl: At Sinai the blood of the covenant made Israel God's family; on the cross and at the altar the blood of Christ seals the new and eternal covenant.
In the Eucharist Jesus gives us his true Body and Blood; we adore him, receive him, and go out to become his body for the world.
2027-05-30.resolve: Make one visit to the Blessed Sacrament this week and stay in thanksgiving after every Communion.
